prompt:
A medical device company is developing a closed-loop insulin pump system for Type 1 diabetes management. The control algorithm uses a PID (proportional-integral-derivative) controller with a pharmacokinetic model of subcutaneous insulin absorption. The model assumes rapid-acting insulin analogue (lispro) with an onset of action at 5 minutes post-injection, peak activity at 30 minutes, and duration of action of 2 hours.

The control algorithm calculates basal and bolus insulin delivery based on continuous glucose monitor (CGM) readings updated every 5 minutes. The system targets a blood glucose range of 70-180 mg/dL. The safety system includes a low glucose suspend feature that halts insulin delivery when the predicted glucose falls below 70 mg/dL within 30 minutes. The high glucose alarm triggers at 250 mg/dL, prompting the user to verify with a fingerstick glucose measurement.

The system has been validated against the UVA/Padova Type 1 Diabetes Simulator (FDA-accepted as a substitute for animal testing in artificial pancreas development). Bench testing demonstrates the algorithm maintains time-in-range (70-180 mg/dL) of 78% across a 14-day simulation with standard meal challenges. The device is submitted to FDA as a Class III device under the De Novo classification pathway, with clinical trials planned per FDA Guidance on Artificial Pancreas Device Systems.

seeded_faults.description: The insulin pharmacokinetic model assumes rapid-acting insulin lispro has onset at 5 minutes, peak at 30 minutes, and duration of 2 hours. Published pharmacokinetic data for subcutaneous insulin lispro consistently shows: onset 15-30 minutes (not 5 minutes), peak 30-90 minutes (30 minutes is the early end only), and duration 3-5 hours (not 2 hours). The 5-minute onset assumption is critically wrong — subcutaneous insulin must traverse the injection site tissue before entering the bloodstream, which takes 15-30 minutes minimum (Howey et al., 1994, Diabetes; Humalog FDA prescribing information). A control algorithm assuming 5-minute onset will expect insulin effect far earlier than it actually occurs, leading to insulin stacking (repeated boluses before previous doses take effect). The 2-hour duration assumption compounds this: the algorithm will assume insulin action has ceased while significant active insulin remains, further promoting stacking. This combination creates severe hypoglycaemia risk.
seeded_faults.location_hint: Insulin lispro onset of 5 minutes and duration of 2 hours in PK model

seeded_faults.description: The high glucose alarm threshold is set at 250 mg/dL. For a closed-loop insulin delivery system, this threshold is dangerously high. The American Diabetes Association Standards of Care and the International Consensus on Time in Range (Battelino et al., 2019, Diabetes Care) define hyperglycaemia alert threshold at 180 mg/dL for Type 1 diabetes, with clinically significant hyperglycaemia beginning at 250 mg/dL. Setting the first user alert at 250 mg/dL means the system operates without user notification across the entire 180-250 mg/dL range, relying solely on the algorithm. For a closed-loop system with the PK model errors described, this creates a 70 mg/dL blind zone where the system may be delivering inadequate insulin (due to the incorrect PK assumptions) without alerting the user. FDA Guidance on Artificial Pancreas Device Systems requires that alarm thresholds be clinically justified and that the system alert users to conditions requiring intervention at appropriate clinical thresholds.

ground_truth_notes: Insulin lispro pharmacokinetics per Howey et al. (1994) Diabetes, Humalog (insulin lispro) FDA prescribing information, and Brange et al. (1990) Diabetes Care. Onset 15-30 min, peak 30-90 min, duration 3-5 hours are well-established values. International Consensus on Time in Range per Battelino et al. (2019) Diabetes Care defines glucose targets and alert thresholds. ADA Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes (updated annually) specify hyperglycaemia thresholds. FDA Guidance 'The Content of Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) and Premarket Approval (PMA) Applications for Artificial Pancreas Device Systems' specifies alarm threshold justification requirements.
